A vignette to demonstrate a planned contrast analysis for 2 x 2
between-subjects designs with simple effects. This vignette follows the
example in chapter 4 of @bird2004. In following this procedure, one may
examine simple effects contrasts to analyse cell mean differences at one
level of a factor by the level (or levels) of the other factor while
controlling the FWER at ⍺. This can be achieved through defining two
families - the A and B Simple Effects Families - which allows one to
examine either (but not both) A or B simple effects. Alternatively, and
as demonstrated in this vignette, one may define a single non-standard
all-factorial contrasts family, allowing for investigation of simple
effects, main effects and interaction effects across all families. In
doing so, one maximises power as compared to a traditional F-STP
approach to simple effects analysis.

## The Packages

To use PsyR to calculate simultaneous confidence intervals, we will
utilise a workflow with functions from
[afex](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/afex/versions/1.4-1) to
implement ANOVA models, and
[emmeans](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/) to obtain estimated
marginal means and the required contrast estimates. So let's load those
packages, and any others that are helpful for our workflow.

```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(afex)
library(emmeans)
library(PsyR)
library(tidyverse)
```

## The Data

The `drive_sleepy` dataframe contains the results of a between-subjects
experiment examining the impact of sleep deprivation and vehicle noise,
vibration and harshness (NVH) on driving performance. Sleep deprivation
has J = 2 levels: twelve or zero hours of sleep deprivation. NVH has K =
2 levels: high or low NVH. The dependent variable is driving performance
as operationalised by a driving errors score, where a higher score is
indicative of poorer performance.

Let's load the data, then call the `head()` function to print the first
5 rows.

```{r loaddata}
data(drive_sleepy)
head(drive_sleepy, 5)
```

To learn more about the `drive_sleepy` dataframe call the help function
using `?df` to open its documentation.

```{r what_sleepy, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
?drive_sleepy
```

Also, let's tidy up the data, labeling the levels of our independent
variable for greater clarity.

```{r longform}
drive_sleepy <- drive_sleepy %>%
  mutate(
    sleep_deprivation = factor(sleep_deprivation),
    sleep_deprivation = fct_recode(sleep_deprivation, "Zero Hours" = "0", "Twelve Hours" = "12"),
    sleep_deprivation = fct_relevel(sleep_deprivation, "Twelve Hours", "Zero Hours"),
    nvh = factor(nvh),
    nvh = fct_relevel(nvh, "high", "low")
  )
```

Next, let's visualise our data. Doing so allows us to more intuitively
understand its layout.

```{r graphit, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dev = 'svg'}
drive_sleepy |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = nvh, y = performance, colour = sleep_deprivation, shape = sleep_deprivation)) +
    stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3, aes(group = sleep_deprivation)) +
    stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", aes(group = sleep_deprivation)) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 14) 
```

## The Analysis

Let's prepare to run some statistical tests!

Here we will create the building blocks for first an ANOVA output, and
later our SCIs. To start, let's run our ANOVA and save it in the `mod`
object. Of note, defining mod in this way enables emmeans to compute
estimated marginal means from which to apply contrasts of interest.

```{r model, message = FALSE}
mod <- aov_ez(
  "subID",
  "performance",
  drive_sleepy,
  between = c("sleep_deprivation", "nvh")
)
```

Time to define our contrasts!

Assembly of contrasts in this design will follow a slightly different
workflow to other designs without simple effects. Following the
Studentized Maximum Root (SMR) procedure outlined on pages 353 and 354
of @bird2005, we will place our contrasts of interest into a set of
lists and then define our SMR parameters based on our family of models
(A(b), B(a), or A(b) $\cap$\$\\cap\$ B(a)).

Let's start by defining our between-subjects contrasts. To do so, create
`btwn_cont`, an object which takes in a list of the following contrasts:

- "Sleep_Dep" ➞ The difference between twelve hours and zero hours of
  sleep deprivation, holding NVH constant.

- "NVH" ➞ The difference between high and low levels of NVH (which, as a
  reminder, is vehicle noise, vibration and harshness), holding sleep
  deprivation constant.

```{r, between_subjects_contrasts}
btwn_cont <- list(
  "Sleep_Dep" = c(0.5, -0.5, 0.5, -0.5),
  "NVH" = c(0.5, 0.5, -0.5, -0.5)
)
```

With our between-contrasts list established, let's obtain our estimated
marginal means. To do so, create the `emms` object and call `emmeans()`
, taking in our previously made `mod` in the "object" argument and a
vector containing our independent variables in the "specs" argument.
Let's also create the main effects object `mfx`, using the `contrast()`
function and placing `emms` in the "object" argument and `btwn_cont` in
the "interaction" argument. This `mfx` object will be important for when
we apply our SMR correction later down the track.

```{r contrasts}
emms <- emmeans(mod, c("sleep_deprivation", "nvh"))
mfx <- contrast(emms, btwn_cont)
```

We also need our interaction contrast. For the sake of clarity we define
it separately in this vignette, but it is also possible to add this
contrast to the above `btwn_cont` list.

- "int" ➞ The interaction between sleep deprivation and NVH. (expand
  later)

```{r interaction_contrast}
int <- contrast(
  emms, 
  list("int" = c(0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 0.5))
)
```

Finally, let's produce simple effects contrasts of NVH at each level of
sleep deprivation and sleep deprivation at each level of NVH. First,
create the `nvh_by_sleep_dep` object. This takes in a model which
attempts to predict our previously made `mod` (which, as a reminder, is
an ANOVA table containing simultaneous tests of the main effects of
sleep deprivation, NVH and their interaction) by using score on NVH
holding constant sleep deprivation. Next, create the `simp_fx_contrast`
object which will take in a list which compares the two levels of NVH
(high minus low). Finally, create `nvh_simp_fx`, an object containing
two simple effects contrasts examining the effect of NVH in participants
with twelve hours of sleep deprivation versus that same effect in
participants with zero hours of sleep deprivation.

```{r nvh_at_sleep_dep}
nvh_by_sleep_dep <- emmeans(mod, ~ nvh | sleep_deprivation)
simp_fx_contrast  <- list("NVH" = c(1, -1))
nvh_simp_fx <- contrast(nvh_by_sleep_dep, method = simp_fx_contrast)
knitr::kable(nvh_simp_fx, digits = 3)
```

Following similar steps, let's also produce simple effects contrasts of
sleep deprivation at both high and low NVH.

```{r nvh_at_sleep_dep_two}
sleep_dep_by_nvh <- emmeans(mod, ~ sleep_deprivation | nvh)
sdep_simp_fx <- contrast(sleep_dep_by_nvh, method = simp_fx_contrast)
knitr::kable(sdep_simp_fx, digits = 3)
```

Finally, let's apply the SMR correction to all our contrasts and produce
their corresponding confidence intervals. To do so, we first need to
create the `all_fx`, `family_list` and `alphas` objects. `all_fx` takes
in a vector containing our previously made contrasts tables. For
`family_list`, we run some code that creates a list equal to the length
of the `all_fx` object containing "b" at each interval to indicate all
our contrasts are between-subjects. Finally, set `alphas` to the nominal
⍺ = .05. This will then be adjusted by the `psyci()` function to ensure
the alpha is appropriate per contrast.

Next, create the object `smr_params` using the `list()` function. Within
the function call, set p and q according to the guidelines on page 359
of @bird2005. Additionally, you may opt to set values for "n_sim" and
"seed", allowing for future replication of the smr distribution.

Finally, create the `output` object by calling `psyci()`, setting the
following:

- The model is set as the previously made `mod` object, where the model
  must be made using the afex package (and of class afex_aov).

- The contrast_tables argument is set as the previously made `all_fx`
  list.

- The method is set as "smr", constructing confidence intervals
  according to the method set out in pages 359 - 360 of @bird2005. Here,
  $CC = \sqrt{SMR_{⍺*;p,qν_{E}}}$ and CIs are constructed where $\psi$ ∈
  $\hat{\psi}$ ± CC · SE.

- The family list is set as the previously made `family_list` object,
  which contains a list equal in length to the `all_fx` object with a
  "b" at each interval (to indicate between-subjects analysis is
  appropriate). The family_list argument must take in a list of the same
  length as contrast_tables.

- The between_factors argument takes in a list of between-subjects
  factor names for our two independent variables.

- Alpha is set at `alphas` (both here and by default), indicating the
  desired type I error rate. The `psyci()` function will adjust the
  nominal ⍺ to be appropriate per contrast.

```{r SMR_correction}
all_fx <- c(mfx, int, nvh_simp_fx, sdep_simp_fx) 
family_list = as.list(rep("b", length(all_fx)))
alphas = 0.05 # because we adjust by contrast

# because we are testing for A(b) and B(a) (and implicitly for A, B, and AB)
# we define our smr parameters using row 4 of Table 2 of Bird & Hadzi-Pavlovic (2005)
p <- 2 
q <- 2
smr_params <- list(
  p = p,
  q = q,
  n_sim = 100000, # this is also the default
  seed = 42 # set seed if you want to replicate simulation of smr distribution
)

output <- psyci(
  model = mod,
  contrast_tables = all_fx,
  method = "smr",
  family_list = family_list,
  between_factors = list("sleep_deprivation", "nvh"),
  alpha = alphas,
  smr_params = smr_params
) 

output %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  relocate(contrast, sleep_deprivation, nvh) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## The PsyR contribution: Simultaneous Confidence Intervals

A simple effects analysis allows one to isolate and understand an
interaction effect. This method is enhanced by creating SCIs which let a
researcher understand the magnitude of simple effects. This allows for
comparison of effect sizes, giving greater clarity into what is driving
an interaction effect. With reference to the current example's
interaction effect, the following may be said.

There is an interaction between sleep deprivation and NVH (p \< .001);
when comparing participants at twelve hours of sleep deprivation to
those with no sleep deprivation, the effect of high NVH was more
pronounced in non-sleep deprived participants than in those with twelve
hours of sleep deprivation. Specifically, with zero hours of sleep
deprivation, experiencing high levels of NVH as compared to low levels
results in significantly worse driving performance (as the upper limit
of Ab~1~ 10.701 \< the lower limit of Ab~2~ 13.259). Further, when at
twelve hours of sleep deprivation there is insufficient evidence to
suggest that NVH levels cause a difference in driving performance
(-6.101, 2.021). However, participants at zero hours of sleep
deprivation performed significantly worse when experiencing high rather
than low NVH (4.579, 12.701). Thus, the AB interaction effect of sleep
deprivation x NVH seems to be most driven by the simple effect of NVH
levels at each level of sleep deprivation.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = 'center', out.width = '50%'}
knitr::include_graphics("../man/figures/PsyR.png")
```
